trap_description: Splitting a monolith into services that share a single database or require synchronous cascading HTTP calls
bad_example: Service A directly queries Service B's PostgreSQL tables or Service A calls B calls C synchronously
remediation_rule: Ensure each service has its own private database; decouple inter-service communication using events or asynchronous messaging.

trap_description: Attempting distributed ACID transactions or 2PC across microservices over WAN/network boundaries
bad_example: Using distributed XA transactions across REST/gRPC endpoints
remediation_rule: Embrace eventual consistency; use the Saga pattern with explicit business compensating transactions.

trap_description: Creating a global 'common' or 'shared' module that holds mutable domain entities used by all modules
bad_example: Importing shared.models.Order in billing, shipping, and inventory modules
remediation_rule: Enforce strict bounded contexts; each module defines its own minimal DTO representation of external concepts.

trap_description: Breaking a system into 15 microservices before understanding domain boundaries or with a team <5 engineers
bad_example: A 3-person startup managing 12 Kubernetes deployments, API gateways, and distributed tracing
remediation_rule: Default to a Modular Monolith with strict package boundaries; extract microservices only when independent scaling or organizational boundaries demand it.

trap_description: Embedding complex routing, orchestration, or business logic inside API Gateways or Enterprise Service Buses (ESB)
bad_example: Adding pricing calculation or customer verification logic inside Kong/Nginx Lua plugins
remediation_rule: Keep communication channels simple (dumb pipes); keep domain logic and orchestration inside application services (smart endpoints).

trap_description: Adopting Event Sourcing for routine CRUD domains with no audit, legal, or temporal query needs
bad_example: Storing simple user profile settings as an event stream requiring complex read projections
remediation_rule: Use standard relational or document persistence for straightforward state; reserve Event Sourcing for high-stakes financial/logistical domains.
